reference_title: Drilled Shafts: Construction Procedures and LRFD Design Methods

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: Means and methods are the contractor's responsibility; final choice of drilling rigs and tools is made by the contractor based on: subsurface conditions presented in contract documents; site visit observations; contractor's personal experience in similar geology; available equipment; and documented experience from previous local projects. Choice of rigs and tools is critical to project success — minor changes in drilling tool can dramatically change excavation rate. Engineers and inspectors must understand general types of rigs and tools available in the US. Contractor normally provides rig/tool details in the drilled shaft installation plan.
key_points: Contractor responsible for means and methods; tool selection is contractor's risk
Engineers and inspectors must understand rig/tool types to develop appropriate specifications
Contractor provides rig/tool details in the drilled shaft installation plan
Pre-bid exploratory shaft excavation may be warranted to help bidders observe conditions
sections.applicability: All drilled shaft projects; specification development and inspection

sections.title: Drilling Machines
sections.body: [p. 4-1] The machines used for drilling shaft excavation have evolved over the years from primitive mechanical systems (e.g., Figure 4-1 from the 1930s), supplemented by heavy reliance on manual excavation, to sophisticated and powerful hydraulic machines with extensive in-cab instrumentation and controls. Section 4.2 gives an overview of the broad range of drilling machines available in current (2018) U.S. practice: 4.2.1 Overview of Rotary Systems, 4.2.2 Mechanical vs. Hydraulic Systems, 4.2.3 Methods of Mounting Drilling Machine, 4.2.4 Other Excavation Systems and 4.2.5 Summary.
key_points: Machines evolved from primitive mechanical systems with manual excavation to powerful instrumented hydraulic rigs
Subsections cover rotary systems, drive types, mounting methods and other excavation systems
figures: Figure 4-1: An Early Drilled Shaft Machine and Crew
sections.applicability: Tool and equipment selection; specification of contractor installation plan requirements

sections.title: Overview of Rotary Systems
sections.body: [pp. 4-2 to 4-3] Most excavations for drilled shafts in the United States are made by some type of rotary-drilling machine. The machines vary greatly in size and design and in the type of machine on which the rig is mounted. The machine transmits force from the power unit through the rotary to a kelly bar to the tool attached to the end of the kelly (Figure 4-2). The capacity of a drilling rig is often expressed by the maximum torque that can be delivered to the drilling tools and the crowd, or downward force, that can be applied. Other factors, particularly the type and details of the drilling tools, can greatly affect the efficiency of the rig, but torque and crowd are important factors affecting the drilling rate. Torque and crowd are transmitted to the tool by a steel drive shaft, the kelly bar or kelly, with the tool mounted on its bottom. Kellys are usually round or square in cross section and may be a single piece (up to about 60 ft long) or may telescope using multiple inner sections to extend the reach. Square kellys often need a worker to insert a pin to lock the outer bar to the inner telescoping piece; round kellys often include an internal locking mechanism. In some rigs the weight of the kelly and tool provides the crowd; in others hydraulic or mechanical devices add downward force during drilling. Details of individual machines are on manufacturers' websites, and a contractor will normally provide them in the drilled shaft installation plan for a project.
key_points: Most U.S. drilled shafts are excavated with rotary drilling machines
Force path: power unit, rotary, kelly bar, tool (Figure 4-2)
Rig capacity: maximum torque and crowd (downward force)
Kellys: round or square; single piece up to about 60 ft or telescoping
Crowd from the kelly and tool weight, or from hydraulic/mechanical devices
Machine details belong in the contractor's drilled shaft installation plan
sections.applicability: Understanding rotary drilling rigs, kelly bars, torque and crowd when reviewing installation plans

sections.title: Mechanical vs. Hydraulic Systems
sections.body: [p. 4-3] Drilling machines are typically powered by mechanical or hydraulic systems (Figure 4-3). A typical mechanical drive delivers power to the rotary via a direct mechanical drive shaft or sometimes a right angle drive from a multiple speed transmission; it has a long history of use, is mechanically simple and relatively lightweight. Most lightweight truck-mounted rigs use direct drive mechanical systems, as do large crane attachments (Figure 4-2). Hydraulic systems to deliver force to the rotary table have increased in recent years: the high pressures available give a higher torque range, and the hydraulic drive lets the rotary move up and down the mast rather than being fixed by the drive system; the movable rotary can elevate above casing and even be used to install casing. Hydraulic rigs are sometimes heavier and more expensive than a similar size mechanical machine. Mechanical drive systems often apply crowd through a pull-down system on a drive bar atop the kelly, guided within the leads as it travels up and down the mast; the same crowd system can be used with a hydraulic driven kelly, but more often the crowd in a hydraulic system is applied through the rotary.
key_points: Mechanical drive: direct drive shaft or right angle drive; simple, relatively lightweight; most light truck rigs and large crane attachments
Hydraulic drive: higher torque range; rotary moves up and down the mast, can reach above casing and install casing
Hydraulic rigs are sometimes heavier and more expensive
Crowd: pull-down on a drive bar atop the kelly (mechanical), usually through the rotary (hydraulic)
figures: Figure 4-3: Mechanical (left) and Hydraulic (right) Powered Drilling Machines
sections.applicability: Comparing mechanical and hydraulic drilling rigs for a project

sections.title: Methods of Mounting Drilling Machine
sections.body: [p. 4-3] The drilling machine must be mounted on some type of carrier in order to drill and move about the site; the type of carrier affects the versatility of the machine and the efficiency of the overall operation. Drill rigs may be mounted on trucks (4.2.3.1), cranes (4.2.3.2), crawlers (4.2.3.3) or excavators (4.2.3.4), or may be designed to operate directly as a top drive unit mounted onto a casing (4.2.3.6); oscillator and rotator systems for casing are in 4.2.3.5.
key_points: Carrier type affects versatility and efficiency
Truck, crane, crawler and excavator mounts; casing-mounted top drives; oscillators and rotators
sections.applicability: Choosing a rig carrier for site access, headroom and casing handling

sections.title: Truck Mounted Drilling Machines
sections.body: [p. 4-4] Mobility is the greatest advantage of truck-mounted drilling machines, which range widely in size and capability, from small, extremely mobile rigs suited to small holes to large heavy rigs capable of drilling rock (Figure 4-4). Where the site is accessible to rubber-tired vehicles and conditions favor them, drilled shafts can be built very efficiently: with the mast stored horizontally, lighter units move readily along a roadway, and the truck can move to location, erect the derrick, level the rotary table with hydraulic rams and begin drilling within a few minutes. Truck-mounted rigs are normally mechanically driven with a fixed rotary, and so may have limited capability to reach over tall casing or handle tall drilling tools; the space below the rotary table can be increased by placing the rig on a ramped platform, a slow and expensive procedure used only in unusual circumstances, but some truck mounts now have a hydraulic sliding rotary that overcomes many of the older limitations. The secondary line has some lifting capacity, necessarily small because of the limited size of the derrick: tools can be lifted for attachment to and detachment from the kelly, but a service crane is usually needed to handle a rebar cage, tremie or casing; some truck rigs can handle light cages and tremies of limited length.
key_points: Greatest advantage: mobility; set up and drilling within minutes
Normally mechanically driven with a fixed rotary: limited reach over tall casing or tall tools
Some now have a hydraulic sliding rotary
Small secondary-line capacity: a service crane is usually needed for cages, tremies and casing
sections.applicability: Truck-mounted rigs on accessible sites

sections.title: Crane Mounted Drilling Machines
sections.body: [p. 4-5] A power unit, rotary table and kelly can be mounted separately on a crane of the contractor's choice (Figure 4-5). Crane mounted rigs can have substantial capabilities and versatility on a bridge project, especially over water, but are less mobile than truck units, and mobilization generally requires rigging or assembly with significant cost and effort. Power units of various sizes can supply large torque at slow rotational speeds. The downward force is usually the dead weight of the drill string, which can be increased with heavy drill pipe (drill collars), doughnuts or a heavy cylinder; special rigging is available to apply crowd for drilling hard rock, and the kelly cross section can be increased for high crowds. The bridge that supports the power unit and rotary table varies widely: with an extended mount the rotary table may be 75 ft or more from the base of the crane boom, which makes crane mounted machines very attractive in marine construction from a barge or work trestle, and the bridge can be built so that a tool of almost any height fits beneath the rotary table, so units with high bridges can work casing into the ground while drilling or take tall tools. A service crane or the drilling crane itself handles rebar cages, tremies, concrete buckets and casings; the secondary lift line on the drilling crane can be used for common lifting by tilting the derrick forward and away from the rotary table, making the unit highly versatile.
key_points: Separate power unit, rotary table and kelly on a crane; strong for bridges and over water
Less mobile; mobilization needs rigging
Crowd from drill string dead weight, increased with drill collars, doughnuts or a heavy cylinder; special rigging for hard rock
Rotary table can be 75 ft or more from the boom base; high bridges take casing or tall tools
Secondary lift line makes the drilling crane a versatile lifting tool
sections.applicability: Crane-mounted rigs for bridge and marine drilled shaft work

sections.title: Crawler Mounted Drilling Machines
sections.body: [p. 4-6] Crawler mounted drilling machines may be less mobile than truck mounted equipment for accessible sites, but provide excellent mobility on the jobsite. Compared with a crane mounted rig, the drilling equipment is usually a permanent fixture on the crawler, with a fixed mast serving as the lead for the rotary or kelly guide system. The crawler mount is the most common system for hydraulic powered rigs, and is also popular for conventional mechanical rigs. Lightweight crawler mounted machines can be extremely versatile on difficult to access sites for slope stabilization, sound wall foundations, and foundations for signs, towers or transmission lines (Figure 4-6).
key_points: Excellent on-site mobility; equipment permanently fixed with a fixed mast
Most common mount for hydraulic rigs, also used for mechanical rigs
Lightweight crawlers suit difficult access: slope stabilization, sound walls, signs, towers, transmission lines
sections.applicability: Crawler-mounted rigs, including lightweight units for difficult access

sections.title: Excavator Mounted Drilling Machines
sections.body: [p. 4-6] The drilling machine can be placed on the arm of an excavator (Figure 4-7); these rigs are almost always hydraulic, using the excavator's hydraulic system. The rig can reach a difficult to access location with low headroom or with limited access immediately adjacent to the hole. Low headroom equipment is often an advantage for a sound wall under overhead utility lines, or when installing shafts below or very near an existing bridge. It has obvious limitations in the depth and size of hole that can be drilled efficiently, and reduced productivity under low overhead conditions will affect costs.
key_points: Excavator-arm mounted, almost always hydraulic
Reaches low-headroom or restricted locations (under utilities, below or near bridges)
Limited depth and hole size; lower productivity affects cost
figures: Figure 4-7: Excavator Mounted Drilling Machines for Restricted Overhead Conditions
sections.applicability: Low-headroom and restricted-access drilled shaft construction

sections.title: Oscillator/Rotator Systems
sections.body: [p. 4-8] Oscillator and rotator systems are hydraulic-driven tools for advancing and extracting casing, often segmental pipe with bolted joints. The machine grips the casing with powerful hydraulic jaws and twists it while other cylinders apply upward or downward force; an oscillator twists back and forth, while a rotator (a more expensive machine) can rotate the casing through a full 360 deg (oscillator with segmental casing, Figure 4-8; rotator installing permanent casing into rock, Figure 4-9). The twisting force must be resisted by a reaction system: the oscillator in Figure 4-8 is resisted by an arm to a large crane whose dead weight gives track friction on a pile-supported work trestle. The force pushing the casing down is normally the dead weight of casing plus machine, but the force to pull it out (which may be much larger once the casing is embedded and partly or completely filled with concrete) must be resisted by the trestle or by the bearing capacity of the ground surface on land; the axial and torque capacity of the whole reaction system must be carefully designed (normally by the contractor). Excavation within the casing is often by clam or hammergrab, although a rotary machine can be mounted on the casing as a top-drive unit, and sand can be removed with a dredge pump or airlift; care is needed not to remove soil below the casing and, as with any circulation drilling, fluid must be pumped in fast enough to keep a positive head of water. These systems are often used with a fully cased hole, although the excavation can be extended into rock or stable soils below the casing.
key_points: Hydraulic jaws grip and twist (often segmental, bolted) casing; oscillator back and forth, rotator full 360 deg
Reaction system must resist torque and the pull-out force, which may be much larger than the push
Reaction system capacity designed, normally by the contractor
Excavation inside by clam, hammergrab, top-drive rotary, dredge pump or airlift; keep a positive water head and do not mine below the casing
sections.applicability: Advancing and extracting segmental or permanent casing with oscillators or rotators

sections.title: Casing Mounted Top-Drive Systems
sections.body: [p. 4-9] Casing mounted top-drive systems are used with reverse circulation drilling, the rotary machine being mounted on the casing itself. A full-face rotary cutting head breaks up the soil or rock, and an airlift pumps the drilling fluid with spoil away from the cutting surface; the fluid is circulated through a desander and/or settling basin and returned to the excavation. Slurry or water may be used, depending on hole stability and casing length. Figure 4-10 shows a top-drive system on the Fore River Bridge in Massachusetts: cuttings rise through the central pipe, the swivel at the top of the drill string and the discharge hose to a spoil barge, and short sections of drill pipe are added as the hole advances; Figure 4-11 shows the cutting head and lowest drill string. The top drive reacts against the casing, so the casing must be embedded sufficiently into firm soil to give a stable platform. The excavation below the casing must be stable to support the casing and to avoid collapse of soil or rock above the cutting head, which could make the head difficult or impossible to retrieve. The casing may be installed with a vibratory or impact hammer or an oscillator/rotator.
key_points: Reverse circulation: full-face cutting head, airlift removes cuttings; fluid cleaned and returned
Slurry or water depending on hole stability and casing length
Top drive reacts against the casing: casing must be embedded in firm soil
Collapse above the cutting head can trap it
Casing installed by vibratory or impact hammer or oscillator/rotator
figures: Figure 4-11: Reverse Circulation Cutting Heads for Top-Drive Drill
sections.applicability: Reverse circulation drilling with casing-mounted top-drive units, often over water

sections.title: Other Excavation Systems
sections.body: [pp. 4-10 to 4-11] Although the vast majority of drilled shafts are excavated by rotary machines, other systems may be used, including manual techniques and excavation with grab tools or slurry wall equipment. Manual excavation (vertical mining, Figure 4-12) is still viable in some circumstances, such as underpinning existing structures; it requires great attention to safety and is usually expensive, and is usually considered only where mechanized equipment is ineffective or the location is inaccessible (to remove a boulder or rock, or in a confined space). In dry excavations into very strong rock, hand excavation might be used, e.g., to penetrate steeply sloping rock such as pinnacled limestone where ordinary tools cannot make a purchase. Safety precautions must be strictly enforced: the overburden restrained against collapse, the water table lowered if necessary, and fresh air circulated to the bottom of the hole. Other non-rotary techniques include a grab, clam or hydromill, as for rectangular diaphragm wall panels; an individual panel used as a foundation is often called a barrette. Barrettes can be oriented to resist large horizontal shear and overturning as well as axial load and can be post-grouted (use and testing in Hong Kong: Ng and Lei, 2003); a barrette is typically excavated under mineral slurry. Clam systems (Figure 4-13) may have a hydraulically controlled guide to keep alignment. A hydromill (hydrofraise in Europe, Figure 4-14), or cutter, typically excavates rock with two counter-rotating wheels at its base, the cuttings lifted by airlift or pump circulating the slurry as in the reverse circulation drill of 4.2.3.6.
key_points: Manual excavation: for underpinning, boulders, confined spaces or pinnacled rock; costly, strict safety (overburden support, dewatering, fresh air)
Barrettes: diaphragm wall panels used as foundations, excavated under mineral slurry; resist shear and overturning; can be post-grouted
Clams with hydraulic guides; hydromills cut rock with counter-rotating wheels and reverse circulation
figures: Figure 4-13: Excavation of a Diaphragm Wall or Barrette Using a Clam
Figure 4-14: Excavation of a Diaphragm Wall or Barrette Using a Hydromill
sections.applicability: Non-rotary excavation: hand mining, clams, hydromills and barrettes

sections.title: Summary
sections.body: [p. 4-11] The variety of machines reflects the maturation of the foundation drilling industry and specialized equipment developed for particular applications. The range of mounting systems and the torque and crowd of modern equipment have extended the size, depth and applications of drilled shafts far beyond those considered feasible a few decades ago. Still, the most common method for the majority of drilled foundations for transportation structures is a simple rotary machine turning a tool at the bottom of the hole and removing soil or rock one auger or bucketful at a time. The machine's capabilities are critical to completing the excavation to the size and depth required, but the choice of drilling tools is often as (or more) important to productivity; tools are in 4.3.
key_points: Modern mounts, torque and crowd have greatly extended drilled shaft size and depth
Most transportation shafts: a simple rotary rig removing one auger or bucketful at a time
Tool choice is often as important as the machine, or more
sections.applicability: Overview of drilling machine selection

sections.title: Tools for Excavation
sections.body: [p. 4-12] Tools for excavation are described under 4.3.1 Rotary Tools (augers, drilling buckets, core barrels, full-faced and special rotary tools) and 4.3.2 Percussion and Other Tools (clamshells, hammergrabs, rock breakers and drop chisels, downhole impact hammers, blasting).
key_points: Rotary tools in 4.3.1; percussion and other tools in 4.3.2
sections.applicability: Tool selection based on soil/rock type and groundwater conditions

sections.title: Rotary Tools
sections.body: [pp. 4-12 to 4-13] The tool selected for rotary drilling may be one of several types depending on the type and physical properties of the soil or rock: augers, buckets, coring barrels, full faced rotary rock tools and other specialized tools. Rotary tools are typically available in 6 inch increments up to approximately 10 ft in diameter, with larger sizes for special cases. Small details in tool design can make a huge difference: for example, the lower portion of the tool must cut a hole slightly larger than the upper part to prevent binding and excessive friction, and one driller may reach refusal with a tool while another makes good progress after a slight adjustment. Contractors and drillers select different tools and set them up in their own ways; important details in apparently similar tools vary, and not all standard tools can be described.
key_points: Augers, buckets, core barrels, full-faced and special rotary tools
Sizes typically in 6 inch increments up to about 10 ft diameter
The bottom of the tool must cut slightly larger than the top to prevent binding
Small tool adjustments can change progress dramatically
sections.applicability: Selecting rotary drilling tools for soil and rock

sections.title: Augers
sections.body: [p. 4-13] Augers can drill a variety of soil and rock types and conditions and are most effective in soils with some cohesion and rock of low to moderate strength and hardness. The cutting edge breaks the soil or rips the rock during rotation, the cuttings travel up the flights, and the auger is withdrawn and emptied by spinning. Difficulties arise in cohesionless sands, where soil slides off the flights, and in some cohesive soils where the tool clogs. Augers vary with the material; earth augers are in 4.3.1.1.1 and rock augers in 4.3.1.1.2.
key_points: Most effective in soils with some cohesion and low to moderate strength rock
Cuttings travel up the flights; auger withdrawn and spun to empty
Problems: sand sliding off the flights; clogging in some cohesive soils
sections.applicability: Auger drilling in soil and soft rock

sections.title: Earth Augers
sections.body: [pp. 4-13 to 4-16] Earth augers may have a single or double cutting surface (Figures 4-15 and 4-16), and many have a central point or stinger that prevents wobbling. Double-flight augers are usually used for stronger geomaterials than single-flight augers; some are true double flight augers and some have a dummy flight giving a double cutting surface that feeds a single flight. The stinger on a single-flight auger is typically more substantial, since it sustains a greater unbalanced moment during cutting. Double flight augers are generally preferred for large diameter holes (Figure 4-17) so that the cutting resistance on the base is more evenly balanced, and some contractors use double-flight augers without stingers efficiently. Flighting must let cut material move up without undue resistance; augers with a slight cup shape can hold soils better under slurry. The type, cupping, number and pitch of flights are chosen for the soil. Auger length governs the material removed per pass and may be limited by the machine's torque and/or lifting capability; longer augers drill straighter holes but are heavier to hoist. Most augers cut a roughly flat base. The teeth in Figures 4-15 and 4-16 are flat-nosed for soil or decomposed rock; the rounded teeth in Figure 4-17 rip harder material; changing tooth pitch by a few degrees can significantly change the excavation rate, and the contractor may need to experiment. In soils or rock containing or derived from clay, softened soil or degraded rock is often smeared on the sides of otherwise dry holes as cuttings are brought up, most troublesome when free water is present from seeps or from water the contractor adds to make cuttings sticky; smear can significantly reduce side resistance, particularly in rock sockets. A simple remedy is to reposition the outermost teeth to face outward and rotate the auger to scrape the sides before final cleanout and concreting. Inserting and extracting augers in drilling fluid can produce positive (insertion) and negative (extraction) pressures that destabilize the hole; side teeth that cut a hole larger than the tool help slurry pass, and tools may have slurry bypass ports (a bypass sleeve around the kelly connection, Figure 4-18). Cobbles or small boulders can sometimes be removed by conventional augers; tapered single-helix boulder rooters (Figure 4-19), sometimes with a calyx bucket on top, are often more successful. A large boulder is difficult: if solidly embedded it can be cored; if loosely embedded coring may be ineffective and it may need breaking by impact or by hand, or lifting with a grab or by cable after a rock bolt is attached.
key_points: Single or double cutting surface; stinger prevents wobble; double flight for stronger material and large diameters
Cupped augers hold soil better under slurry; length limited by torque and lift, longer augers drill straighter
Flat-nosed teeth for soil and decomposed rock, rounded teeth to rip harder material; tooth pitch matters
Clay smear on hole walls can significantly reduce side resistance, especially in rock sockets; scrape with outward-facing teeth before concreting
Auger insertion/extraction in slurry causes pressure surges; use oversize side teeth or bypass ports
Boulder rooters for small boulders; large boulders cored, broken or lifted
figures: Figure 4-17: Large Diameter Auger with Double Cutting Edge
sections.applicability: Earth auger selection, sidewall smear and slurry pressure surges

sections.title: Rock Augers
sections.body: [pp. 4-16 to 4-17] A flight auger specially designed for rock can drill relatively soft rock (hard shale, sandstone, soft limestone, decomposed rock), using hard-surfaced conical teeth usually of tungsten carbide. Rock augers are often double-helix, with thicker flights than soil augers (Figure 4-20); tooth geometry and pitch are important, oriented to promote chipping, and rock augers can be tapered. Some contractors make pilot holes with a tapered auger smaller than (perhaps one-half of) the borehole diameter and then excavate to the final diameter with a larger flat-bottom rock auger or core barrel; the stress relief often makes the final excavation much easier. Tapered rock augers do not produce a flat-bottomed hole, and an unlevel base can be harder to clean and to make a sound bearing surface.
key_points: For relatively soft rock; conical tungsten carbide teeth; often double helix with thick flights
Pilot hole about one-half the diameter eases final excavation
Tapered augers leave an unlevel base that is harder to clean
sections.applicability: Drilling soft rock with rock augers and pilot holes

sections.title: Drilling Buckets
sections.body: [pp. 4-17 to 4-18] Drilling buckets are used mainly in soil, as they are not effective in rock. The rotary digging action forces soil into the bucket through two slots in the bottom, and flaps prevent it falling out (Figure 4-21); the tool is withdrawn and the hinged bottom opened to empty the spoil. Buckets are particularly efficient in granular soils, where an open-helix auger cannot bring the soils out, and under drilling slurry, where soils slide off augers; under slurry the bucket should have channels so slurry passes freely without excess positive or negative pressure below the tool, which is often easier to provide on buckets than on augers. Flat-nosed teeth gouge the soil; where cemented layers or rock occur within the soil, conical ripping teeth may replace one row of flat teeth to drill alternating soil and rock without changing tools. Drilling buckets are generally not appropriate for cleaning the base. Muck buckets or clean-out buckets (Figure 4-22) clean the base with water or slurry in the hole, using cutting blades rather than teeth for more effective removal and a more uniform bottom; their closure flaps or plates are critical, since soil falling out defeats the cleaning, and they should have pressure-relief channels when used under slurry.
key_points: For soil only; efficient in granular soils and under slurry
Slurry channels prevent pressure surges below the tool
Conical ripping teeth can be swapped in for cemented layers
Drilling buckets do not clean the base; clean-out (muck) buckets with blades and tight flaps do
sections.applicability: Bucket drilling and base cleanout in soil, dry or under slurry

sections.title: Core Barrels
sections.body: [pp. 4-19 to 4-21] If augers are ineffective in rock (e.g., too hard), most contractors next try a core barrel. Coring loads the cutting bits more effectively, the crowd being spread over the perimeter rather than the whole face. Ideally the tube cores until a discontinuity is reached and the core breaks off; the core is held in the tube by friction from the cuttings, lifted out, and deposited by shaking or hammering the barrel or occasionally by splitting it with a chisel. The simplest core barrel is a single cylindrical steel tube with hard metal teeth on the bottom edge (Figure 4-23), with no direct means of removing chips; teeth are staggered to avoid tracking in one groove and to cut slightly larger than the tool: chisel teeth for soft rock, conical points for harder rock, button teeth for harder rock where conical points break off; the oscillator/rotator casing is a type of core barrel that commonly uses button teeth. In hard rock with significant penetration, a double walled core barrel may be more effective; these are more expensive and can have roller bits as well as teeth (Figure 4-24). Cuttings are removed by circulating air in a dry hole or water in a wet hole through the space between the walls; double-walled barrels can extract longer cores than single-walled ones, which constantly twist and fracture the rock without fluid to remove cuttings. Loosening and recovering the core (Figure 4-25) after a few feet of penetration is a problem: if it breaks at a horizontal seam it may be lifted directly or by a rapid turn of the tool; a hydraulic device can grab a core; otherwise a chisel is driven into the annulus to break the core off or into pieces. Blasting may be used to break up a core where permitted, and a hammergrab or clamshell can lift loose or broken cores.
key_points: Next choice when augers fail in rock; crowd concentrated on the perimeter
Single wall barrels: chisel teeth (soft rock), conical points (harder), button teeth (harder still); oscillator casing is a core barrel
Double wall barrels: air or water circulation removes cuttings; longer cores
Core recovery: lift at a seam, hydraulic grab, chisel in the annulus, blasting where permitted, hammergrab or clamshell
sections.applicability: Coring rock for drilled shaft sockets and recovering cores

sections.title: Full-Faced Rotary Tools
sections.body: [p. 4-22] Full face rotary tools may be used for drilling rock, particularly at large depth. The tools in Figure 4-26 carry roller bits across the entire cutting face; the bits grind the rock, which is flushed to the surface by reverse circulation (4.2.3.6). Disk shaped cutter heads or teeth have been used with full face tools in soft rock or cemented soils. Full face tools have occasionally been used with direct circulation in small diameter holes (less than 30 inch) in hard rock, compressed air down the center of the drill string blowing the cuttings out.
key_points: Roller bits across the whole face grind rock; cuttings removed by reverse circulation
Disk cutters or teeth in soft rock or cemented soils
Direct air circulation occasionally in hard rock holes under 30 inch
sections.applicability: Full-face rotary drilling of rock at depth

sections.title: Special Rotary Tools
sections.body: [p. 4-23] Suppliers and contractors have developed many special tools for unusual problems. The tool on the left of Figure 4-27 cuts grooves in the borehole walls to help develop the shearing strength of the soil or rock along the shaft sides; the core barrel on the right has steel wire on the outside to scrape cuttings or loose rock (usually degradable shale) from rock socket surfaces, known regionally as a backscratcher. Figure 4-28 shows the Glover Rock-Grab, which cores and then grabs rock to lift it, sometimes effective for boulders or fragmented rock where augers or core barrels fail. Numerous other special tools are developed for specific projects.
key_points: Grooving tool roughens the socket wall to develop side shear
Backscratcher scrapes cuttings and loose shale from socket walls
Boulder-grabber (Glover Rock-Grab) cores then lifts boulders or fragmented rock
figures: Figure 4-27: Special Rotary Tools: Grooving Tool (left) and "Backscratcher" (right)
sections.applicability: Special tools for socket roughening, cleaning and boulder removal

sections.title: Percussion and Other Tools
sections.body: [p. 4-24] In contrast to rotary drilling, percussion drilling breaks up rock, boulders or cemented soil by impact; the broken material is removed with a clamshell-type bucket or by other means such as air circulation. The tools range from simple, crude drop tools to sophisticated hammer drills.
key_points: Percussion breaks material by impact; removal by clamshell or air circulation
sections.applicability: Percussion and non-rotary excavation tools

sections.title: Clamshell or Grab Bucket
sections.body: [pp. 4-24 to 4-25] Bucket excavation starts with setting a guide for the tools, corresponding to a surface casing in rotary work; the guide may be circular or rectangular to suit the tool, and excavations can have various shapes and be quite large. With oscillator/rotator systems (4.2.3.5) the segmental casing is the guide; for diaphragm walls or barrettes (4.2.4) a guide-wall is often built at the surface. The tools are handled either on a cable from a crane (cable tool), the jaws opened and closed by a second cable or a hydraulic system, or on a solid rod (a kelly that does not rotate but moves up and down in guides), again with a mechanism to open and close the jaws. Clamshells or grab buckets are used where rotary tools are unproductive or impractical, e.g., for broken rock, cobbles and loose soils that the bucket can pick up; hard massive rock or boulders are first broken with a rock breaker and then lifted. A circular clamshell is shown on the left of Figure 4-29; clamshells and grabs come in diameters up to about 6 ft and can make noncircular excavations (right of Figure 4-29), the tool conforming to the guides.
key_points: A guide (casing, guide-wall) is set first
Handled by cable (cable tool) or by a non-rotating kelly
For broken rock, cobbles and loose soil; massive rock broken first
Diameters up to about 6 ft; noncircular shapes possible
sections.applicability: Clamshell and grab excavation for shafts and barrettes

sections.title: Hammergrabs
sections.body: [p. 4-25] Hammergrabs are percussion tools that both break and lift rock (Figure 4-30). They are made heavy with dead weight; the jaws close when the tool is dropped and the wedge of closed jaws breaks the rock, and the hardened teeth open to the full size of the tool to pick up the broken rock. They are heavy and relatively expensive, but unlike rock breakers and clamshells the tool need not be changed to lift the broken rock, which speeds excavation. Hammergrabs can also build noncircular barrettes by changing the length of the long side.
key_points: Break and lift rock without changing tools
Heavy and relatively expensive; faster than breaker plus clamshell
Can build noncircular barrettes
sections.applicability: Breaking and removing rock with hammergrabs

sections.title: Rock Breakers and Drop Chisels
sections.body: [p. 4-26] Rock breakers and drop chisels (Figure 4-31) are heavy objects lifted and dropped to break boulders, cores and strong soils so the material can be lifted by a clamshell or grab bucket, or to break rock at the bottom of the hole to advance it more easily; several types are dropped by a crane. Chisels have a single point to break off a core or a boulder or ledge on the side of the hole. Rock breakers in Figure 4-31 include the churn drill and star drill, with a wedge-shaped bottom to produce high stresses in the rock. Broken pieces are removed with a clam or hammergrab, or sometimes a rotary auger.
key_points: Dropped heavy tools break boulders, cores, strong soil or rock at the base
Chisels break off cores, boulders or ledges; churn and star drills have wedge-shaped bottoms
Debris removed by clam, hammergrab or auger
figures: Figure 4-31: Drop Chisels and Rock Breakers
sections.applicability: Breaking obstructions and rock by impact

sections.title: Downhole Impact Hammers
sections.body: [p. 4-26] To excavate hard rock across the full face, a large diameter downhole hammer can make an excavation up to about 7 ft in diameter through very hard rock such as granite (Figure 4-32; the tool at left is a cluster of air-operated hammers, a cluster drill). Downhole hammers are typically used for rock that has proven extremely difficult to remove by core barrels or other means; the debris is typically blown out with air if the hole is dry. This is extremely expensive, and rock sockets in such hard material are best avoided, especially in urban areas where rock dust can be a hazard.
key_points: Full-face excavation up to about 7 ft diameter in very hard rock (granite)
Used where core barrels fail; debris blown out with air in dry holes
Extremely expensive; avoid sockets in such rock, especially in urban areas (rock dust)
sections.applicability: Excavating very hard rock with downhole hammers

sections.title: Blasting
sections.body: [p. 4-28] Blasting is usually not permitted for drilled shaft excavation because of the safety hazard and the potential for fracturing the surrounding bearing formation, which could harm the foundation's performance. Explosives may be considered on rare occasions to aid hand excavation of rock near the surface, e.g., to break through a boulder or obstruction in the hole, through small predrilled holes to level a steeply sloping surface so casing can be seated, or through hard pinnacle limestone above the zone relied on for capacity. Primer cord wrapped around the base of a core at the bottom of the kerf has reportedly broken cores away successfully, a small shock not thought to affect the surrounding rock. Highly expansive cements have occasionally been used instead of explosives, placed in small air-track holes to split the rock. Explosives must be handled by experts and used only with the permission of the regulating authorities.
key_points: Usually not permitted: safety and fracturing of the bearing formation
Rare uses: boulders or obstructions, leveling sloping rock to seat casing, pinnacle limestone above the bearing zone
Primer cord around a core base; expansive cements as an alternative
Experts only, with regulators' permission
sections.applicability: When explosives may be considered in drilled shaft excavation

sections.title: Other Techniques
sections.body: [p. 4-28] Other techniques: 4.4.1 Tools for Cleaning the Base of the Drilled Shaft Excavation and 4.4.2 Methods for Stabilizing Soils or Formation.
key_points: Base cleaning tools in 4.4.1; ground stabilization in 4.4.2
sections.applicability: Wet construction base cleanout; challenging soil conditions

sections.title: Tools for Cleaning the Base of the Drilled Shaft Excavation
sections.body: [pp. 4-28 to 4-29] Besides the clean-out buckets of 4.3.1.2, non-rotary tools are useful for removing cuttings and debris from the base, most commonly a pump (Figure 4-33). The air-lift pump (left) pumps air down a supply line alongside the air-lift pipe; air entering the pipe a few feet above the bottom lifts the fluid column, and the buoyant lift causes suction at the bottom that lifts sand or loose material. The hydraulic pump (right) uses two hydraulic lines to rotate an impeller that pumps fluid up from its base; it is more controllable than an airlift (volume and velocity more easily regulated), while airlifts tend to remove larger particles. Pumping systems are probably the most effective way to remove loose cuttings or debris from the base of a wet hole, but their aggressive use in cohesionless sands can advance the excavation. The effectiveness of base cleanout in wet holes is best evaluated with a downhole camera (Section 15.2.4).
key_points: Airlift: air injected a few feet above the bottom lifts fluid and debris; removes larger particles
Hydraulic pump: impeller, more controllable volume and velocity
Most effective cleanout for wet holes, but aggressive use in sand advances the hole
Check cleanout with a downhole camera (15.2.4)
figures: Figure 4-33: Airlift and Hydraulic Pumps for Shaft Base Cleanout
sections.applicability: Cleaning the base of wet drilled shaft excavations

sections.title: Methods for Stabilizing Soils or Formation
sections.body: [p. 4-29] On rare occasions, permeation or compaction grouting may be used to stabilize a particularly unstable stratum or around a very large or deep hole. Baker et al. (1982) report that grouting in advance of excavation can sometimes reduce water inflow effectively and even permit under-reams in granular soil, with successful examples in Chicago. Grouting to enhance base resistance in granular soils is in Chapter 3. Skin grouting through sleeve-port tubes along the side of the shaft has been used on rare occasions internationally but is rarely employed in U.S. practice.
key_points: Permeation or compaction grouting, rarely, to stabilize unstable strata or around large or deep holes
Grouting ahead of excavation can cut inflow and allow under-reams in granular soil (Baker et al., 1982, Chicago)
Base grouting: Chapter 3; sleeve-port skin grouting rare in U.S. practice
sections.applicability: Pre-excavation grouting of unstable ground around drilled shafts

sections.title: Summary
sections.body: Chapter described drilling machines and tools for drilled shaft construction. Choice of tools and equipment is generally the contractor's responsibility. Engineers must be knowledgeable of drilling equipment to provide appropriate specifications, constructable and cost-efficient designs, and sufficient subsurface information for bidders. Tools and equipment planned by contractor should be described in the drilled shaft installation plan and documented in construction records.
key_points: Contractor's drilled shaft installation plan must describe planned tools and equipment
Engineers must understand equipment to write appropriate specifications
Sufficient subsurface information required for bidders to make informed equipment decisions
sections.applicability: Overview of Chapter 4, Tools and Equipment.
